The game is relatively similar to Orwell, which I enjoyed very much. It got some clever gameplay aspects to it and most of the puzzles are neither too easy nor too hard. The storylines, while a bit predictable at times, are fine and easy enough to follow. Also, the voice actors do a pretty good job for a game of this scope. 

Why the thumbs down then? Because the game really suffers from the fact that the writers and developers don't seem to be fluent in the English language. Unfortunately, this leads to grammatical errors, a strange choice of words and stilted dialogues at every corner, which constantly breaks the immersion and sometimes even makes it hard to understand what the game is trying to tell you. In a game mostly relying on text, this is a huge issue. Getting native speakers on board to help with the translation could help a great deal, I think. Considering this game is in Early Access, I'd gladly turn this negative review into a positive one, if the language problem gets fixed.

"Cyber Manhunt" is a visual novel disguised as a detective game: it has a few timed puzzles and optional information, but in general the game is linear.
The story is far from perfect: it is too dark and not depressing enough at the same time to be realistic. The ending chapter is just meh. The gameplay has a few shortcomings: the in-game desktop is not responsive enough, the data gathering process is tedious, and the puzzles can be bothersome given the running timer. The stylization is fine, I guess, until it comes to anything computer-related (Of course, it is of little importance, but now I know that viruses are always written in C and bash while any database with private data utilizes systemd. Wait. What?) The English translation is sub-par and has lots of typos.
It is a bit sad, because I see the potential in this game, but I cannot recommend it.

First and foremost, this is NOT a hacking game. It is a hacking THEMED puzzle game. It's one of those types of hacking games where there's clearly a specific path forward, but the technology in-game is not consistent with the real world so you're forced to act as the game expects and not rely on your technical expertise or intuition. This might be fine for people who don't know anything about computers, though, but I have worked in IT for over 20 years and find this extremely aggravating as I enjoy actual hacking games and detective/mystery stories where I can put that to use. It doesn't need to be literally analogous to the real world, but there's a certain aptitude you develop in IT that aids you in trying to figure things out and none of that is applicable here. 

For example, email addresses unrelated to what you're doing are masked, which is not consistent with the platform since you can see related emails. You have the ability to search using the resources provided (search engine, database), but you can't search for emails that the game doesn't want you to search for, even though it's directly related to the task at hand and would be a way to get the solution you're looking for in the real world. Another example, in the tutorial mission, I accidentally skipped past a point of dialogue where the woman has given you the next task, but since the game is presented very rigidly I can't for the life of me figure out what the game is looking for, and your hands are tied despite having the "web" and database to search through. Searching the "web" only works when it's extremely specific to the case, and searching an email address should pull up a ton of info but this is not an option due to it not being what the game is specifically expecting. Anyone familiar with technology would be able to tell you that there's always multiple ways to get the information, but the game does not allow for this. It's a puzzle to figure out, not hacking. As far as hacking goes, it was a stereotypical fantasy magically-get-the-answer thing to click. No technical knowledge needed, and in my case it worked against me.

The translations or pronunciations of technical jargon are off, enough to also be aggravating if you're familiar with the terms. Non-tech folks likely won't notice, but it makes me wonder who the game's target audience is? Games like these should be about immersion, and they snap you out of it quickly and it's very obvious that this is in no way related to hacking or the tech industry.

After playing for just a few minutes it was the complete opposite of what I was expecting in an entirely negative way. It reminds me of Orwell, but Orwell had much better presentation and design and wasn't trying to be something it's not. I actually enjoyed Orwell a lot but it was clear it was in the Orwell fantasy world, so it was logically consistent. This game mimics real world applications in a way that is completely misleading and jarring, and equally inconsistent. 

Do some heavy research before purchase. If you're technical, hard pass, there's too much suspension of disbelief and plenty of other hacking games to choose from that are better suited. If you're not technical, and you enjoy puzzles and the idea of movie hacking, you might like it.

I don't mean to sound cruel, but I'm shocked that is game is so highly rated at the time of my review as it is marred by several critical flaws. 

Most glaringly, the English translation and localisation is atrocious. Considering this is coming from a non-native English speaking studio, I was willing to overlook some of the inaccuracies since there is a lot of text you have to sift through, but even some of the phrases in the "connecting the dots" puzzles, the crux of the game, are unintelligible, and could only solved after looking up the solution. The voice acting is painfully subpar and its apparent that they were not given much direction for their performance. While I don't mind when a game explores dark subject matter, the discovery of the plot is often sapped of any suspense when the villain(s) often brag the same way Dr. Doofenshmirtz does with his evil inventions.

Even if you plan to not play this game in English, I would still recommend avoiding as you will spend the entire game clicking away at every sentence on every site in case it has a meaningful clue to record, as they are the very puzzle pieces you will need to literally connect later. There is more I can say about the game, but I think you get the picture. Instead, consider getting "The Roottrees are Dead" if you want to get your internet sleuth on.

review_text_raw:
I normally avoid leaving negative reviews on games that didn't work for me. The way I see it, my personal dislike of particular features or plot points doesn't necessarily add up to a bad game for someone else. Unfortunately, in the case of Cyber Manhunt, I feel justified in leaving this review because I think the game fails at what it sets out to do: making the player feel like a hacker solving a compelling mystery.

The first, and perhaps greatest challenge to immersion I encountered here is the writing. To clarify, my primary issue is not with the English translation. I do believe there are many odd choices that add up to very stilted and unnatural-sounding conversations, but I would have been able to see past this if the characters and stories involved were more thoughtfully written to begin with. 

Most of the characters you investigate in Cyber Manhunt embody one-dimensional stereotypes. This makes the stories you uncover about them highly predictable. The social issues the game claims to focus on (according to the blurb: cyber violence and privacy breaches) are explored in what I personally believe to be an equally shallow, one-dimensional way. There are also additional social issues, such as sexual violence and human trafficking, which I believe the writers were simply not equipped to handle at all—and I say that as someone who has had to deal with these issues in my past work. The behaviour of both the victims and the perpetrators is painfully unrealistic, to the point that I suspect the writers took more inspiration from internet creepypastas than real life cases. 

Because the puzzles rely on narrative complexity to be interesting, I believe the game falls flat on this front as well. You scour social media accounts, emails and webpages for names and other personally identifiable information. Databases and password cracking tools help you access more data to scour. There are occasionally phishing sequences where you select dialogue choices. All of these mechanics have the potential to be a fun, highly simplified social hacking simulation, and I can see Cyber Manhunt is trying its best to do just that. I even believe it might have worked—if there was more thought put into how the characters communicate and what their motivations might be as full-fledged human beings. A predictable story with one-dimensional characters who speak and write in a stilted, unnatural sounding way just doesn't make for a very engaging data-scouring experience.

All in all, I am disappointed with the wasted potential in Cyber Manhunt. I hope that if the devs go on to make more narrative games, they will make quality writing a higher priority of the overall experience.

So, as others have said I picked this up originally as it looked quite similar to Orwell. It had a lot of the same ideas and actually was a bit more creative in some aspects but it really fell short when it came to the story. I played the demo and was intrigued and ended up buying the game and while I don't regret it I can't see myself playing through it again or recommending anyone to play through it without knowing the issues that it has. We'll start with the Cons:

1. While yes, the English is not perfect - it's not game breaking by any means and apart from a few funny lines (liver streamer??) it really didn't affect my game that much. Definitely not the biggest weakness of the game.

2. The stories for each of the chapters were very unique but they got more complex as time went on and ended up just being confusing (again this could be a language issue?). Lots of times I was finding information out about the stories that was telling what actually happened only for it to be ignored and unable to be collected. It felt like we weren't getting the true aspect of the story and that was hinted at later in the game but nothing ever happened with this? For example - It's highly alluded to that [spoiler] Jim and Isabella killed Austin multiple times. But nothing ever confirms this and I don't know what the point of alluding to it was if it's never confirmed. [/spoiler] It felt like they were throwing twists at you just to throw twists at you, and they ended up not making much sense.

3 - The endgame was a MESS. Dates going in weird orders, changes happening to the story that didn't make sense and it left me feeling really unsatisfied. Trying to complete every chapter to 100% was so rough, not collecting one snippet of an email you checked at the beginning of a chapter could be your downfall for the next three hours... And instead of having a hint system you can choose to use, you're left to going back through everything you've already been through throwing your cursor around looking for a red box. It takes away from the story and is boring gameplay. Definitely would be better to be able to contact Ashley for a hint when you're stuck.

Pros:

1 - Look I beat the game and it is certainly not the worst game I've ever played. I enjoyed the good parts of the game. Each chapter was super unique, the game wasn't afraid to go a bit dark, and it did have SOME good twists thrown in.

2 - The voice lines were pretty clear and had very little grammatical mistakes. Quite good voice acting and added to the characters - unfortunately there weren't loads of them but the ones that were there really added to the games vibe.

3 - It is the closest thing to Orwell I've found and I appreciated the game play and the way the devs tried to adapt it to change it up as the chapters progressed. 

If you're desperately looking for something like Orwell then get the demo and see if it's your thing. But otherwise I really can't recommend the game right now.

I enjoy mystery/investigation and hacking games, so I was looking forward to trying this one out for a while. That said, I didn't have high expectations going in to this game because it doesn't cost that much. 
However, I wouldn't recommend this game for the following reasons:

1. My choices didn't matter and there was only one correct answer. I was excited to play this because I thought it would have a multi-layered investigation, like "The Roottress are Dead," but it's far short of that. Grabbing data from various documents is the main mechanic, which lead to "inferences," which are mostly guesswork to get the right answer so you can go forward. There were no consequences to getting something wrong, thus no multiple endings.

2. The story lines for the two missions I played were kinda gross to me. [spoiler] Both centered on blond, white women. In the first mission, the woman lied about her domestic abuse and scammed multiple husbands. And in the second the woman was a college student who was forced to be a "sex slave." This trite theme was repulsive to me and not fleshed out in an interesting way.[/spoiler] I quit playing because I lost interest in the overarching story or how the missions were connected.

3. The scripts (and some of the corresponding voice acting) were really bad. They didn't suit the characters at all, so much so that it broke my immersion.

Really disappointed about this game. I was hoping for some good sleuthing, but as I've read in other reviews the game soon becomes hovering your mouse over text to find predefined clues, reading content optional. All other game mechanics reach like 10% of their potential:
- "googling" for clues: you can really only search for people's names, everything else returns "not found"
- hacking passwords: copy/paste info from another window and click the button
- phishing: you have to trial and error until you find the random sequence they imagined
Aside from that, getting into emails and other accounts, all gets repetitive really fast. 
About translations: I read about other reviewers complaining about the English. When I purchased the game they had just released improved translations, but there is still much work to do...
Last point: what I would have liked to see, is a much more open gameplay, where one has to read everything to find clues, take their own notes, and has chances to make mistakes so that there is at least an illusion that the path to success isn't linear.

review_text_raw:
I want to like this, but there are a number of things that make it hard to recommend this:

* A majority of the game involves finding text that will highlight in red when you click it to allow you to "gather clues" -- which leads to clicking every line of text, just in case. At some points, you'll be missing a single clue and have to go slogging back through all that you've previously read to find the one little sentence or phrase that you didn't click to highlight and collect. 
* The translation to English is absolutely terrible. In some places, that actually makes trying to figure out what the game wants you to do more difficult.  
* There's also some comically bad voice acting at times. To make matters worse YOU CAN'T FUCKING SKIP the spoken dialogue scenes. This is particularly egregious because in many sections you have to listen to entire conversations before you can collect any of the evidence (that is, click every sentence trying to find what will be highlighted in red as clues). 
* At some points, you're asked to piece together what happens, but you CAN'T TAB BACK TO WHERE THE INFO YOU COLLECTED IS STORED TO FIND THOSE ANSWERS!
* While it can be satisfying to poke around to get the info you need in the investigation stages, some of the other minigames/puzzles are just not fun to play. This is particularly bad when you reach the final stage(s) of the game. I was on my way to 100% completion, but that final stage is a such a slog of *TIMED* minigames, I stopped playing the main story and moved on to the DLC (they were cheap, so I thought I'd give them a try).
* A few stages are timed, and although some portions are generous with how much time you're given, it definitely makes it far less fun.
* The main story takes a twist that is just... asinine. [spoiler] You discover you're not a real person, but an AI--just like the antagonist. [/spoiler] Seriously, it killed the immersion the gameplay and story had managed to build.

It's a very low cost game, and I did get some fun out of it--but I don't think I can, in good conscience, recommend it to others.

The English is challenged. The creators do not understand how the internet works. If I type-in Defoss, for example, I should still get search results. In a news article, the company's name is Defoss then Devos. These are not the full name of the company, and without the full name, you get no results when you search. 

When you do a new search, sometimes it opens a new tab, other times, it closes a tab you had open. It's unspeakably annoying! MY browser doesn't behave that way; never did, not even NetScape.

There is a part of the game where you have to guess what approaches are going to work best with insane or mentally-unstable people. You can choose between "appease", "intimidate", or "ask for the truth", for example. Now, none of these yield results the first time. There is some secret combination of these that you have to figure-out. You have three tries. You do not know enough about this person to understand how they will react, because they ARE mentally-unstable.

What do I dislike the most? Once you are into any screen like the inference screen, a phone call, hacking, etc., you cannot back out and have no access to your notes; you also cannot escape. I was wanting to double-check someone's interests, but was not allowed to close it or escape it. I wanted to double-check data I had collected while making a phone call. Not being a mind-reader, I didn't know ahead of time what I would be asked. IRL I would be able to retrieve the information upon being asked, like re-visiting a website.

That is not fun. The typo of the company name is highly annoying in a game, where you are searching for clues, as is the inability to search the company name and be shown results. This needs an overhaul.

Really wish I could recommend this game but the bugs and poor translation ruin what would have otherwise been a cool experience. Ran into two game breaking bugs, one fixed after a reset and the other remains to be fixed, in the last chapter. After solving a puzzle the game reverts back to a state before the puzzle was solved, while the timer continues to countdown.

Another huge problem, especially in the last chapter, is the game is throwing a ton of background lore at you while an onscreen timer ticks away, in a scenario where the game can't even be paused. The interface already makes it hard to quickly grab information, but now you have to grab it while racing the clock, and solving puzzles. Your option is either to go slow and actually absorb the lore (failing and having to repeat after multiple attempts), or go quickly and miss anything story related. 

The concept of this game is great and almost done well here. ALMOST. It needs better translation and better writing, way less bugs and a better UI. Whether it was script or direction, the voice acting was not up to par either.

Playing for so long only for the game to break at the end really soured me on it, but I'm hoping the devs can fix it for their next iteration, because there is definite potential here.

This game has a couple of problems:
1. Some of the things you have to deduce are really far fetched. Like:
[spoiler]You're supposed to figure out which limb a person has injured by assuming that all people are right handed[/spoiler]. I needed to look that up, after like 20 minutes.
2. To get the achievement for each chapter you have to get all the evidence and the only way to get evidence is to hover over every text, because if it is evidence it will be marked red. This can be turned of in the settings, but that just makes it even harder!
3. While doing a dialogue you may need to know things along the lines of 'when does this person do x?' and you can't look it up while doing the dialogue which mean it's basically 'choose something random; it's the wrong choice; look it up; advance dialogue; repeat'. I'm sorry but it can't remember every minute detail that may or may not be relevant in a dialogue tree, 30 minutes down the line.
4. QoL features I wish the game had. These are not really a problem but would be nice:
  - The back, forward and reload buttons in the browser don't work.
  - You can't enter URLs in the browser
  - Sometimes the browser opens new tabs, sometimes it doesn't. Would be nice if 'new tab' was bound to middle mouse button and 'open here' to left click.
  - The password cracker, which seems to be made to be like a dictionary attack thingie, doesn't crack the password unless it has ALL information even if the information isn't contained in the password e.g. 
  "Name: Susi"
  "Date of birth: 1.1.1970"
  resulting password is '111970"
  It wouldn't need the name for that.
  - Sometimes text messages appear on both sides of account and sometimes they're only on one side e.g.
  You lock into Alice's and Bob's account and on Alice's account the conversation is
  A: "Hi long time no see"
  B: "Are you ghosting me?"
  
  And on Bob's account it's
  A: "Hi long time no see"
  B: "Are you ghosting me?"
  one day later
  B: "Sorry. Didn't see your messages. Here's the super secret info you need."
  A: "Thank you"
  - Calling a person before you're supposed to just tells you that they're not available currently.
  - Hacking things is less like a puzzle and more of 'type this into a text box, then you have 5 minutes to find what you want and if you don't succeed you restart and have to type the text into the box again'. Like it's actually type a text into a box. It's 'this is the password `ERGT467´ type this into the text box below'. The time limit just seems pointless and the having to repeat everything after you run out of time seems frustrating.

Due to story content I can not recommend this game.

There are clear translation errors both linguistically and probably culturally but those can be fixed. There is a prologue and 5 chapters and each chapter is a good length for a gaming session. The prologue and Chapters 1, 3, and 4 are quite interesting with the end of Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 being where the game shines.

Nor was I prepared that part way through Chapter 5 you read a website about human trafficking and animal abuse. You get one "clue" from that website and it tells you a little bit about the plot, but both points are brought up later in a much less graphic and traumatizing way. If I hadn't guessed that Chapter 5 was the last chapter I would have quit the game right there. 

If the game was just the prologue and Chapters 1, 3, 4, and the end sequence of Chapter 5, I would highly recommend this game. If the animal abuse and human trafficking parts of Chapter 5 were not there in any way shape or form, I would recommend the game with some caveats. With the story as is, I can not recommend that people play it. Chapter 5 made me feel violated, and that I had not consented to what it put me through. If I had known the plot I would not have bought this game. 

Due to story content I can not recommend this game.

review_text_raw:
I was 80% of the way to giving this a thumbs because hey, it's ten bucks and it will kill a few hours of your life, the puzzles are somewhat challenging and clicking around playing pretend-hacker is always diverting.

It doesn't quite get over the finish line for a few reasons:

As much there are ominous warnings about sensitive subject matter and deep thoughts concerning your privacy, the game is REALLY rough from a narrative standpoint. The game is translated from Chinese, and while their English is a great deal better than my non-existent Mandarin, it's still not good, with really clunky dialogue that kills any emotional heft the story may be going for and some variable (but mostly bad) voice acting. And when you're tackling serious topics like sexual assault and bullying and online harassment and such, you shouldn't be giggling at deadpan "he attacked me like an animal" deliveries. In other words, don't expect to lose yourself in the story here.

But whatever, it's a budget game, they couldn't shell out for a localization team, that's forgivable. You can still have a good time playing pretend-hacker and solving puzzles, right?

Well... you could have, maybe, if the game weren't so full of bugs. Some are merely annoying, like someone asking you over the phone the name they used when they e-mailed you and you put in that name and they say it's wrong, so you double-check and look for one of the two other options there, but you don't see it, so you throw your hands up, look at a guide, see the answer, look again at the e-mail wondering where they ever used the name and then just put it in because you've already wasted ten minutes and just want to get on with it. Someone quizzes you on what part of their body was injured, and that information was never made available anywhere. You can try these puzzles repeatedly, but you can't back out if you fail and go double-check stuff again, you have to go all the way out to the main menu and then re-continue the game.

None of this was enough to turn me off the game until I hit Chapter 5. Without going into details, Chapter 5 was so buggy, it forced me to quit and re-load the game three times, and finally reached a point where I really couldn't progress because a specific tool I needed to finish a puzzle wouldn't load. By that point, I was done.

What inevitably earns this game the thumbs down is just that there are much better hacking games and "surveillance is bad" games out there. TIS-100, Hacknet, Grey Hack, Orwell. Even if this game is cheaper, go spend the extra money elsewhere. It will be worth it.

review_text_raw:
TL;DR: What it lacks in interesting mechanics it makes up for in repetetiveness.

Slightly longer review: 

You google names, go to their facebook page, click on interesting info and then google that, or enter it into the same five programs while the UI makes you wait for 10 seconds every time you found a hint. Then you answer some exams to check if you paid attention. If you expect deductions or logic puzzles, you will not find those here. It is all simply about reading and remembering information.

Sometimes there are minigames but they are also not interesting. One in particular really sucks, because you simply aren't given the information necessary to make the correct decisions, so you just click on random stuff until it somehow works.

It is one of those games where I suffered through the last 3 hours because I wanted to see the ending, but I had my head in my hands a couple times because it was just so annoying sometimes.

The writing.. well first of all, from a purely technical standpoint, it is bad. Clearly whoever wrote this is not fluent in english. There are tons of typos and grammatical errors all over the place. Things which could have easily been fixed by proofreading. Funnily, it gets better torwards the end. Or I just stopped paying attention, which is probably more likely.

From a stroy perspective, it is actually *ok*. Not great, not terrible. There were definitely some good parts, some twists, and some hateable characters. The main issue is that the gameplay is so boring that torwards the end you just use your mouse to scan over text really quickly to find hints, and stop actually reading it.

Overall score: meh/5.

I wanted to like this game as it's clear that quite a bit of effort was put into making it, and (at least at the date of this review) the developer is still trying to improve on it.  The graphics are nice and I like this genre of game.  Game play length is decent, you can complete it within 9-10 hours at a leisurely pace.

Having said that, I can't bring myself to recommend it.  The worst part of the game is the writing. Aside from some translation and grammatical errors which I can ignore, the nicest way I can put it is that the writing style is simply not for me. The characters are so incredibly tropey, dramatic and honestly cringey in the way they speak. The twists and turns are juvenile and the themes are simplistic and shallow. The game doesn't say anything you don't already know (i.e. wouldn't it be bad if hackers are able to use your private data on social media for nefarious means? Really makes you think!).

Aside from the writing, the game play is okay though fairly repetitive.  The game does try to keep you engaged with new mini games that pop up, though at least one puzzle right at the end of the game is completely frustrating in a way that makes no sense and when you're under time pressure as well. By that point, I just wanted the game to be finished.

I'm sure there's an audience for this game (maybe younger people?) but it's not for me unfortunately.

review_text_raw:
Cyber Manhunt is a take on an Orwell style game, but it lacks the polish and quality of those titles. Sometimes you can find a piece of information that you need (for example, a character's name) earlier in a chapter, but the game won't let you 'learn' it until you reach a later point because it isn't the specific place where the game wants you to collect that information. Certain dialogue choices are vague and their outcomes are unpredictable. Sometimes the game will ask you to provide specific information that you collected (or information that the game never clearly gave) but won't let you access your 'notes'.

There are a few interesting minigames scattered throughout, but some of them give a strict time limit and vague guidance as to what you need to do. Failure just sets you back a short time, but in some instances you're forced to sit through unskippable dialogue scenes to get back to the minigame.

There are a lot of good ideas here, and the chapters and overall story are fairly interesting, but the overall presentation makes this more of a frustrating experience than a fun one.

review_text_raw:
Mostly a hacking game about copy and pasting information from one box to another. I think there's a good idea here somewhere, but the execution is lacking. I like the idea of information gathering from social media and other open information sources. However, only the clues that are important from the game's perspective really matter and they're only found by mousing over in-game text or images, so you're really running your mouse over everything by habit, and there are few opportunities to really make impactful decisions.

A game like this could do well if the writing and setting are done well, but the situations presented so far seem really contrived. Combine that with dialog that sounds awkward and stilted, with word choices and grammar that were obviously not written or proofread by a native English speaker and it really takes you out of the game. What I've seen so far is not broken English, more awkward English, like it was translated automatically.

Most other reviews paint a good picture with similar information, so I think it comes down to personal preference. Overall I agree this game plays more like a visual novel and less like a puzzle game.
